text: West Prussia was once a province between the Baltic Sea and the Vistula River. For centuries,
it was a region of strategic importance, economic opportunity, and cultural diversity. Its history
was shaped by competing powers, changing borders, and the lives of people who often
had little influence over the decisions made above them. To understand what happened here,
we have to go back several centuries. During the Middle Ages, the Teutonic Order
expanded into the region. Over time, it established a powerful state, building castles, founding towns,
and controlling important trade routes along the Baltic coast. But its power was challenged by
the Kingdom of Poland and Lithuania. After decades of conflict, the Second Peace of Thorn
in 1466 divided the Order's territory. The western part came under the Polish Crown and
became known as Royal Prussia. The eastern territories remained under the Teutonic Order.
This division would shape the region for generations.
In the 18th century, the balance of power changed once again. In 1772, Prussia, Russia,
and Austria carried out the First Partition of Poland. Large areas of what would later become
West Prussia were taken by the Kingdom of Prussia. Danzig and Thorn initially remained
outside Prussian control. That changed in 1793, when both cities were incorporated during the
Second Partition of Poland. West Prussia was now firmly part of the Prussian state.
The region developed economically and administratively. Agriculture, trade,
and industry became important parts of everyday life. Danzig remained a major commercial center,
while the Vistula connected inland territories with the Baltic Sea.
Yet beneath this development, national, cultural, and political differences remained.
Then came the First World War. In 1918, the German Empire collapsed.
Poland regained its independence after more than a century of partition and foreign rule.
The question of borders became one of the most difficult issues in the post-war settlement.
Under the Treaty of Versailles in 1919, large parts of West Prussia were transferred to Poland.
The newly established Polish state gained access to the Baltic Sea through the territory known
as the Polish Corridor. This created a geographical separation between Germany and East Prussia.
Danzig received a special status. It became the Free City of Danzig under the protection
of the League of Nations. It was no longer part of Germany, but it was also not incorporated
into Poland. Other areas remained disputed. In the Marienwerder Plebiscite of 1920,
the overwhelming majority voted to remain with Germany. The historic province of West
Prussia was dissolved. Its former territories were divided between Germany, Poland, and the
separate administration of Danzig. For the people who lived there, these decisions had
immediate consequences. Trade routes changed. Administrative systems were reorganized.
Families and communities found themselves separated by new international borders.
During the interwar years, relations between Germany and Poland remained tense. Danzig became
a focal point of political conflict, while the Polish government invested in the development
of Gdynia as an alternative Baltic port. The region increasingly became part of a wider struggle
over national identity, economic interests, and political influence. In September 1939,
Nazi Germany invaded Poland. Danzig was annexed by Germany, and the surrounding territories were
incorporated into the German Reich. The occupation brought systematic persecution,
violence, and mass murder. Polish political, religious, and intellectual leaders were
targeted. Jewish communities were destroyed as part of the Holocaust. Thousands of people were
imprisoned, deported, or murdered. The region became deeply involved in the crimes of Nazi
Germany. By 1945, the Second World War had devastated much of Europe. As Soviet forces
advanced, large numbers of civilians fled westwards. Many others were displaced after
the fighting ended. At the end of the war, the territories east of the Oder-Neisse line came
under Polish administration, pending a final peace settlement. The German population was expelled
or displaced. At the same time, Polish families arrived, many of them having themselves been
forced to leave territories in eastern Poland that had been annexed by the Soviet Union.
The population, language, and cultural landscape of the region changed fundamentally. For those
who had lived there for generations, the end of the war meant the loss of their homes and
familiar surroundings. For those arriving, it meant beginning a new life in a place
transformed by war and displacement. The old province of West Prussia no longer existed.
Its cities, roads, churches, and landscapes remained, but the political and social world
that had shaped them for centuries had largely disappeared. Today, West Prussia is a historical
region divided between modern-day Poland and Germany. Its past cannot be reduced to a simple
story of one nation against another. It is a history of changing borders, competing identities,
political decisions, and human consequences. To understand West Prussia is to understand how
profoundly European history could change the lives of ordinary people, and how the traces
of those changes remain visible long after the borders themselves have disappeared.
